messages.text: Take {gift_item}. A good village keeps its friends fed and standing.
Here, {gift_item}. It is honest work to send someone off with provisions.
Good. {tested_villager} has a sound nose for {gift_item}. Fresh advice, clean cut.
If {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}, then the cut was right.
Bad cut, then. For {gift_subject}, I would set down {gift_item} and bring {alternative_gift}.
Some gifts spoil in the telling. Try {alternative_gift}; that should suit {gift_subject} better.
You got a tough cut of advice. Next time, bring {alternative_gift}.
{gift_item} went over badly? Then trim your losses and try {alternative_gift}.

openings.text: Mind the smokehouse. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to keeping meat salted and safe, then.

lines.text: A smokehouse tells you fast who understands patience.
Empty hooks before supper can frighten a village more than thunder.
Food decides whether a scare becomes a disaster.
If you smell smoke, that is supper being planned properly.
Salt is patient. That is why it keeps food better than most people keep promises.
Empty hooks tell a village to start worrying before anyone says it aloud.
A full cellar has ended more arguments here than any speech ever did.
My jokes are like my cuts: better when nobody rushes me.
That was stale enough to leave on the shelf.
People think about courage until supper is late. Then they think about supper.
A village with good stores can make careful choices instead of desperate ones.
Once the smokehouse door stuck shut, and everyone became helpful very quickly.
I have carved gristle with more grace than you brought here.
I remember hunger without a name. You brought me back before it swallowed everything.
The cure left me shaking, but alive. That counts for more than a full smokehouse.
Your face stirs something. Not appetite. Memory, I hope.
I remember a sour potion, an apple, and trying not to bite the hand near me.
I remember enough to be grateful, and enough to be ashamed. Give me room.
Thunder shook the smoker so hard the smoker coughed smoke sideways, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked the smoker, hooks, and food barrels after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the smoker, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the food barrels twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have food barrels to set right.
I checked grease, wood, and hanging meat for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the smoker after.
The smoker can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the smoker, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the smoker, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the smoker can go cold; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the smoker still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before the smoker, hooks, and food barrels. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the smoker and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the smoker, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the smoker first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the back door by the smoker and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the smoker enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping salted meat for the watch between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the smoker, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning dust out of the meat barrels.
I checked the smoker, hooks, and food barrels, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the smoker, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a butcher which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the smoker, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The smoker can go cold. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the smoker found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the smoker. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the smoker roof and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the smoker. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.

pacify.text: Fine. I have work to get back to, and anger spoils the day.
Too lean an offer. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds} if you want this cut clean.
No. I know bad meat, and I know bad apologies.
